top_choice_rationale: The magic-wavelength lattice is a specific, checkable idea: the trap shifts both clock levels equally, so many neutral atoms are interrogated without perturbation. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL) reproduce uncertainties near 1e-18 and their comparisons agree, and the results already yield measurements of nature (centimetre-scale gravitational redshift, limits on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings). The allocation to Katori (concept and first strontium lattice clock) and Ye (accuracy, stability and many-body systematics) is clean, and a citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice keeps it separate from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. The novelty overlap with earlier precision-spectroscopy prizes is a real reservation but does not outweigh the achievement, so I rank it above no award.
recusal_note: No direct connection to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile, but I work in neighbouring atomic physics (light shifts, polarisabilities, atomic-structure theory) and collaborate with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, so a possible field-proximity question could be raised.
